ios.desc:
When's my bus? OneBusAway answers that question in real time, at every stop, across your whole region.

Now with Live Activities: start tracking a ride and watch it approach from your Lock Screen, without opening the app.

Free, open source, and built by a nonprofit in partnership with your transit agency.

WHAT'S NEW

- Live Activities — follow your bus, train, or ferry from the Lock Screen and Dynamic Island.
- A redesigned stop view that opens right from the map, putting real-time arrivals one tap away.

FEATURES

- Real-time arrivals wherever your agency provides them.
- Departure alarms that nudge you before your ride pulls away.
- Trip planning with door-to-door directions across every agency in your region.
- See where your vehicle actually is on the map — buses, trains, ferries, streetcars, even funiculars.
- Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets for the routes you check most.
- Bookmarks and recent stops, so your daily commute is always a tap away.
- Nearby stops found automatically, or search by route, address, or stop number.
- Service alerts from your agency, right where you need them.

WHERE ONEBUSAWAY WORKS

- Davis, CA
- New York, NY
- San Diego, CA
- Seattle / Tacoma / Puget Sound, WA
- Tampa, FL
- Washington, D.C.
- Adelaide, Australia

ABOUT

OneBusAway is free and open source, maintained by transit riders and researchers since 2008. There are no ads and no account to create.

The app is published by the Open Transit Software Foundation, an IRS-registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit that has earned Silver Transparency status on Candid.

Questions, feedback, or support: https://onebusaway.org/

OTSF on Candid: https://www.guidestar.org/profile/84-1786969

> Android actually hasn't suffered from tactile UI fragmentation much more than iOS has.

If the apps on this page a representative, I'd say that Android has experienced a lot more UI fragmentation than iOS.  These are being held up as examples of best Android interfaces, and they look very inconsistent to me.

In contrast, I just opened up a bunch of random apps on my phone's home screen, and they all look very much like "iOS style".  Obviously the native apps match well, but so does OneBusAway, Wikipanion, Skype (though the UI is flatter than the rest), Google Voice, Amazon, OneNote, etc.

These all look like iOS apps to me.

I work on a suite of open source public transit software projects, collectively called OneBusAway (or OBA). The software is used by millions of transit riders every day around the world, including in New York City, the Seattle area, San Diego, and Washington, D.C.

Through the non-profit that collectively owns OBA, I've been working on a managed services offering to help transit agencies adopt the software, which has historically been beloved by users, but a real pain to set up and maintain. The software, cleverly named OBA Cloud, turns what used to require a month-long engagement with a transit consulting firm into a 15 minute, wizard-driven process.

The best part is that since all of the software is free and open source, a transit agency that decides they love OBA but wants to be locked back into an expensive contract can always ask a consulting firm to run the software for them.

Since last month[1], we've added a number of great new features to OBA Cloud, like broadcasting critical alerts to all riders in the system via push notification, and support for Live Activities on iOS.

We're hosting four new public transit systems over last month, and are continuing to make terrific strides on our other marquee projects:

The iOS app update went live, and our riders are generally loving it: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/onebusaway/id329380089

The new Android app maintainer is gearing up to release the biggest new version of the app in a decade: …
